title: Piezomagnetism in a model cubic noncollinear altermagnet
authors: Sudarshan Sharma, Luca Buiarelli, Richard Spieker, Ivan Jakovac, Damjan Pelc, Turan Birol, Martin Greven
abstract: Altermagnets constitute a distinct class of magnetic materials that combine compensated magnetic order with spin-polarized electronic bands, hence carrying characteristics of both antiferromagnets and ferromagnets. Piezomagnetism - the linear relationship between lattice strain and a net magnetic moment - has emerged as smoking-gun evidence of altermagnetism that distinguishes it from antiferromagnetism. Here, we uncover a large piezomagnetic response in MnTe2, a cubic altermagnet with a noncollinear spin arrangement and weak spin-orbit coupling. We combine dilatometry with nuclear magnetic resonance, a bulk local probe, to observe signatures of both direct and inverse piezomagnetism consistent with symmetry considerations and first-principles calculations. The dilatometry measurements reveal a shear deformation proportional to an applied magnetic field, while magnetic resonance detects a ferromagnetic moment induced by shear strain. The respective results for the piezomagnetic coupling strength are in good agreement, and they are captured by first-principles results. These findings for simple binary MnTe2 position this material as a model altermagnet, demonstrate the utility of nuclear magnetic resonance in investigations of piezomagnetism, and open new avenues for multimodal strain and magnetic-field control in spintronic and memory applications.
summary: This work demonstrates that piezomagnetism is a definitive signature of altermagnetism, using $	ext{MnTe}_2$ as a model system. By combining dilatometry, NMR, and DFT, the authors successfully measured and confirmed a linear coupling between applied strain and magnetic moment. This opens new avenues for controlling spintronic devices using coupled strain and magnetic fields.
main_problem: The study investigates piezomagnetism—the linear coupling between lattice strain and net magnetic moment—as a key signature distinguishing altermagnetism from conventional antiferromagnetism.
main_result: The authors report observing a large piezomagnetic response in the model cubic altermagnet $	ext{MnTe}_2$, confirmed by agreement between dilatometry measurements (shear strain proportional to $H$) and NMR detection of an induced ferromagnetic moment.
method: The research combines multiple experimental techniques, including dilatometry and NMR, with first-principles Density Functional Theory (DFT) calculations to probe the magnetostrictive and piezomagnetic coupling coefficients.
model_or_system: The system studied is $	ext{MnTe}_2$, a cubic material identified as a model altermagnet possessing compensated magnetic order and spin-polarized bands. The analysis utilizes symmetry constraints derived from the Landau free energy to predict the linear coupling terms.
key_observables: Linear magnetostriction ($\epsilon \propto H$), shear deformation, stress-induced ferromagnetic moment (measured by NMR), and the piezomagnetic coupling coefficient ($\lambda$).
important_parameters: The measurements are sensitive to temperature, particularly near the magnetic transition temperature ($T_N$), and depend on the crystal orientation ($\langle 100 angle$ vs $\langle 110 angle$).
main_assumptions: The linear magnetostriction component is assumed to represent the genuine altermagnetic signature, distinct from quadratic or domain-related contributions. DFT calculations sometimes ignore ion-mediated strain contributions.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the magnetic structure, magnetostriction dependence on applied field along different axes, temperature dependence of the coupling coefficient, and NMR spectra showing line splitting under applied stress.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first establishing the theoretical framework of piezomagnetism in altermagnets, then presenting experimental measurements (dilatometry, NMR) on $	ext{MnTe}_2$ to extract the linear coupling terms, and finally confirming these findings using first-principles DFT calculations.
why_interesting: While focused on condensed matter magnetism, the use of coupled external fields (strain and magnetic field) to control electronic properties is relevant to understanding emergent quantum phenomena in engineered materials, bridging concepts from AMO physics (field control) to solid-state physics.

Figure 1b shows a sketch of the lattice response of cubic MnTe2 to a magnetic field along [001]. For this geometry, an in-plane shear strain is induced with a magnitude that is proportional to the applied field. In other words, there is a linear magnetostriction component along [110], whereas magnetostriction is purely quadratic along [100]. As shown in Fig. 2a and Extended Data Fig. 2, our data confirm these predictions: along [110], the magnetostriction is dominated by a linear magnetic field dependence, while along [100] the response is purely quadratic.
